Casi un año después del anuncio del alto el fuego, las fuerzas israelíes siguen atacando infraestructuras, hospitales y civiles en el enclave palestino. El Ministerio de Sanidad de Gaza calcula que más de 1.400 personas han fallecido desde entonces, y más de 5.000 han resultado heridas por los ataques pese al acuerdo. Dentro de la Franja apenas quedan medicamentos y la entrada de ayuda humanitaria es muy reducida.

“Las inundaciones, las temperaturas extremas y el frío no harán más que agravar los riesgos sanitarios de una población a la que durante años se le ha negado el acceso a una atención médica adecuada y cuyo sistema de salud ha quedado totalmente destrozado”, denuncia Sanbar.

Metodología

Para localizar las fortificaciones militares israelíes en Gaza, hemos desarrollado un sistema de búsqueda visual basado en inteligencia artificial que nos ha permitido identificar estructuras similares entre cientos de imágenes de satélite. Después, hemos revisado y contrastado los resultados para distinguir las posiciones fortificadas de otras construcciones o movimientos de tierra.

En total, hemos analizado más de 600 imágenes de la Franja de Gaza, tomadas entre enero de 2023 y octubre de 2026, que suman más de 400 GB de información. La mayoría proceden de Planet Labs y tienen una resolución aproximada de medio metro por píxel. También hemos utilizado una imagen aérea del norte de Gaza, publicada en la plataforma GovMap del Gobierno de Israel, con una resolución aproximada de 15 centímetros por píxel.

La investigación se ha desarrollado en cinco fases, con sucesivas rondas de búsqueda y revisión:

1. Selección de ejemplos. Escogimos 15 imágenes de fortificaciones con características reconocibles: grandes muros de tierra, accesos protegidos, zanjas y estructuras interiores como barracones, vehículos o antenas. Añadimos otros 15 ejemplos de caminos, excavaciones y terrenos arrasados que podían confundirse con ellas.

2. Búsqueda mediante inteligencia artificial. Dividimos las imágenes en 1.550.108 fragmentos, procedentes de 602 escenas de Planet Labs y de la imagen aérea de GovMap. Desarrollamos una herramienta que comparó estos fragmentos con los ejemplos seleccionados y los ordenó según su similitud. Repetimos las búsquedas incorporando los resultados ya revisados para identificar nuevos candidatos. La inteligencia artificial nos ayudó a localizar posibles fortificaciones, pero no decidió cuáles lo eran.

3. Revisión y evolución temporal. Examinamos las propuestas, descartamos las coincidencias incorrectas y reunimos imágenes de distintas fechas para cada ubicación. Así pudimos reconstruir los cambios visibles en el terreno y observar cuándo aparecían las primeras modificaciones.

4. Comprobación de uso militar. Para distinguir las fortificaciones de otros recintos, buscamos indicios adicionales, especialmente estructuras compatibles con barracones o módulos prefabricados. Revisamos distintas fechas para comprobar si estas instalaciones habían estado presentes, incluso cuando el recinto aparecía posteriormente vacío. Estos elementos, junto con la configuración del terreno, reforzaron la identificación de las posiciones militares.

5. Recuento final. Tras descartar falsos positivos y agrupar las imágenes correspondientes a una misma ubicación, identificamos 50 posiciones fortificadas. Para documentar su evolución, elaboramos 50 series temporales con 4.382 imágenes, accesibles para los lectores de EL PAÍS, después de excluir los recortes sin cobertura suficiente.

Limitaciones de la investigación. La cobertura de las imágenes no es uniforme: no disponemos de todos los lugares en todas las fechas. Por eso, la primera imagen en la que aparece una construcción no indica necesariamente cuándo fue levantada.

Las 50 posiciones identificadas representan las fortificaciones que hemos podido verificar en el material disponible, no un censo exhaustivo de todas las existentes en Gaza. Aunque hemos revisado miles de candidatos, no podemos descartar que haya otras posiciones que nuestra herramienta no haya detectado.

Las imágenes nos permiten documentar las estructuras y su evolución, pero no determinar por sí solas la función exacta de cada instalación ni si estuvo ocupada de manera continua. Para ello necesitamos contrastar nuestras observaciones con otras fuentes.

La 13enne ucraina operata di tumore gli regala un peluche: 'Ti proteggerà'

Un viso limpido ma anche un braccio che alla sua giovane età mostra già un cerotto su una ferita. Si rimarginerà ma le cicatrici sono profonde. Varvara, in italiano Barbara come un po' già si sente, ha solo 13 anni, è ucraina e ha dovuto subire delle cure di tipo oncologico. Ma oggi proprio con Papa Leone ha potuto condividere la gioia di lasciarsi il peggio alle spalle.

"Un sogno realizzato", dice lei stessa ai cronisti aiutata da una interprete e con la mamma che la stringe in un istinto di protezione rafforzato dall'improvvisa ribalta mediatica ricevuta sul piazzale del policlinico Agostino Gemelli. Varvara, appassionata di storia e letteratura ma anche di musica e in particolare della batteria, è stata curata in Italia dove ha trovato rifugio e accoglienza dallo scenario di guerra.

Il 31 dicembre scorso, a margine di un' udienza generale in Piazza San Pietro, malata di tumore e prossima ad una operazione, aveva già potuto abbracciare il Papa dal quale, raccontava, aveva ricevuto "forza e incoraggiamento". In quel momento né lei né di certo Leone avrebbero mai potuto immaginare di reincontrarsi così presto e proprio a causa di una infausta prognosi comune. Varvara ha atteso fin dalla mattinata il Pontefice all'uscita, accompagnata da alcuni familiari e un prete ucraino, padre Taras che è stato tramite prezioso nella sua vicenda. Dal Papa ha ricevuto quella benedizione che cercava ma con lui ha potuto condividere anche qualche parola quasi di conforto vincendole.

La giovane gli ha consegnato quindi i regali che aveva preparato: la foto stampata del loro abbraccio a San Pietro dentro a una cornice nella ceramica tipica di Castellamonte, dove è stata dapprima accolta. E soprattutto un pupazzetto in pannolenci con le sembianze del Pontefice, che lei stessa ha cucito a mano. Un peluche, come quello che si era portata da casa ribattezzato Basik, unico ricordo della vita di prima. "È il solo amico che ho dall'inizio della guerra che mi accompagna e mi accompagnerà in Italia dove non conosco nessuno, dovrò affrontare un lungo percorso in ospedale e lui sarà il fratellino che non ho", aveva raccontato appena arrivata a Torino. Una specie di surrogato, in attesa di quelle amicizie e di quella vita che l'aspetta. Donandolo al Papa gli ha assicurato: "Ti proteggerà".

articles.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
articles.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.
articles.preview: Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks. Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. Trump has denied asking for satellite access to be suspended. Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
articles.body:
Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. Trump has denied asking for satellite access to be suspended.

Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice" and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.

Trump agreed the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.

Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.

"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.

Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.

"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side â and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness â then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.

"I think that is completely wrong."

Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.

The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

Crosetto said that victory for Ukraine would be "a victory for peace, a victory for justice, a victory for international law".

He vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.

The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.

At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".

Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".

But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.

Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.

During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.

Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."

In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.

But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow â targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".

"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."

Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.

The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".

A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.

But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.

"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

articles.title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
articles.summary: The BBC joins Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regains crucial territory in the Donbas, but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.
articles.preview: A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker. Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
articles.body:
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.

This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September â and suffered few casualties in return.

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".

Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.

Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.

Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.

Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.

Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.

The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.

An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."

He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.

Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".

"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.

"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."

"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.

"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvresâ¦ each of these actions is a building block towards victory."

All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.

Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.

But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.

The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.

I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."

articles.preview: Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. A settembre, prima dei droni ucraini, questi contenuti ne avrebbero ottenute milioni.
articles.body:
Altri osservatori, basandosi su proprie analisi, hanno invece sostenuto che, dopo l’attacco ai server russi di Yandex, i contenuti legati alle campagna di disinformazione russa che prendono di mira tematiche come le prossime elezioni presidenziali francesi avrebbero ottenuto su X solo poche decine di migliaia di visualizzazioni. A settembre, prima dei droni ucraini, questi contenuti ne avrebbero ottenute milioni.

Verifiche indipendenti e molti esperti di disinformazione hanno spiegato tuttavia che non esistono ad oggi dati affidabili e verificabili che dimostrino che ci sia stato un calo significativo dell’attività di influenza russa online dopo l’attacco ucraino alle infrastrutture di Yandex.

Cosa dicono le analisi e le indagini indipendenti

Da più parti si è provato subito a fare chiarezza su come andassero interpretati i grafici utilizzati come prova. L’istituto di monitoraggio dei media polacco Emocje w slacieci ha chiarito innanzitutto un concetto, la cui scarsa conoscenza ha favorito il diffondersi di questa narrazione: un bot non è necessariamente un account falso che diffonde propaganda del Cremlino sui social media. Inoltre, nel caso dell’attacco ai server di Yandex, a essere rilevato era stato il crollo dell’attività dei cosiddetti web crawler, ossia i programmi automatici impiegati da ogni motore di ricerca, incluso quello russo di Yandex, per esplorare il web e per indicizzarne i contenuti. La stessa Cloudflare, riporta la BBC, ha chiarito che i suoi dati includono tutte le richieste Internet automatizzate ai siti web ospitati sulla sua rete, compresi i bot che scansionano i siti web alla ricerca di informazioni. L’azienda statunitense ha inoltre specificato all’emittente pubblica che il calo mostrato nel grafico «non è necessariamente dovuto al comportamento dei bot sulle piattaforme dei social media».

Il secondo grafico, invece, quello che avrebbe mostrato il crollo delle attività online riguardanti AfD dopo gli attacchi ucraini, risulta essere privo di qualsiasi riscontro. Il grafico in questione infatti, oltre a non aver alcuna fonte indicata sulla provenienza dei dati e a non risultare chiaro nella dicitura “attività giornaliera”, risulta essere stato pubblicato su Threads per la prima volta l’11 ottobre. Tuttavia, nell’asse orizzontale del diagramma i dati arrivano fino al “15 ottobre”, quindi una data futura.

Agli esperti di disinformazione l’idea che un semplice attacco di questo tipo potesse portare a un crollo delle operazioni di influenza russa è suonata subito molto semplicistica: parlando col Guardian, Ned Mendez, responsabile della ricerca dell’organizzazione Alliance4Europe che si batte contro la disinformazione, ha spiegato che per evitare di essere segnalate come sospette dalle piattaforme, le bot farm operano con modalità che ne favoriscono la distribuzione e la resilienza, per esempio attraverso connessioni residenziali e phone farm. «Non possiamo semplicemente cancellare i bot a forza di bombe, per quanto l’idea possa sembrare allettante», ha dichiarato Mendez.

Vari istituti che analizzano la disinformazione online hanno invece segnalato che, dal canto loro, non era stata individuata nessuna correlazione tra l’attacco ai data center di Yandex e un crollo del traffico di certi account. Come riportato dalla testata tedesca Capital, sia l’Istituto di ricerca Cemas che il think tank Polisphere – entrambi impegnati nell’analisi di disinformazione e nel monitoraggio social di account tedeschi attribuibili ad attori della disinformazione, sostenitori dell’AfD e gruppi di diffusori filoruss – non si sono registrati cali statisticamente significativi dell’attività nei Paesi di lingua tedesca. Sono state dello stesso tenore le affermazioni di altri analisti e del gruppo BotBlocker, specializzato nell’analisi di troll farm russe presenti sulle piattaforme social.

Quando le affermazioni categoriche delle prime ore sono state messe in discussione, non trovando conferme indipendenti, alcuni dei profili che più avevano contribuito a diffondere questa narrazione sono intervenuti di nuovo per scusarsi o ridimensionare la propria posizione iniziale. L’analista militare polacco Jaroslav Wolski che aveva postato il grafico infondato su AfD ha cancellato il tweet e scritto un secondo post sull’argomento: «Purtroppo il mio post contenente disinformazione ha raggiunto milioni di visualizzazioni, e per questo desidero scusarmi ancora una volta con tutti i lettori. Naturalmente mi assumo la piena responsabilità di ciò che ho fatto e, in modo semplice e umano, mi vergogno di avervi disinformato. Chiedo scusa anche agli oppositori che avevo contestato e che sono stati i primi a farmi notare che mi sbagliavo».

Mentre in risposta a una richiesta di informazioni da parte di ZDFheute, l’eurodeputato ceco Zdechovský ha ammesso di non possedere attualmente dati verificabili in modo indipendente che provino in modo definitivo un collegamento tra gli attacchi e un calo dell’attività delle reti di disinformazione russe. «Non ho mai affermato che tale collegamento sia stato definitivamente dimostrato», ha aggiunto.

L’ufficio di Zelensky ha dichiarato alla BBC che il presidente ucraino si riferiva «all’atmosfera sui social media» piuttosto che a una diminuzione dell’attività dei bot, aggiungendo di aver ricevuto «segnalazioni di un minor numero di commenti provocatori e di incitamento all’odio» da parte di molti utenti dei social media.

Le conseguenze provate degli attacchi ucraini

Come abbiamo visto, quindi, non ci sono prove che permettano di concludere che gli attacchi ai data center di Yandex abbiano avuto un impatto sulle operazioni di influenza della Russia. Ma questo non significa che non ci siano state conseguenze in Russia.

Come scrive Meduza – media russo indipendente con sede in Lettonia, bloccato in Russia perché considerato «organizzazione indesiderabile» – i droni ucraini hanno creato interruzioni diffuse su tutta la rete internet russa, bloccando temporaneamente i servizi di Yandex, tra cui Yandex Go, Yandex Eats e Yandex Pay, utilizzati in gran numero di russi. Inoltre, molti altri siti web e servizi sono andati offline, tra cui quelli di importanti banche, rivenditori, marketplace online, piattaforme di annunci classificati, siti web e app di notizie e molto altro. Questo perché queste aziende utilizzavano l’infrastruttura di Yandex per archiviare i propri dati. I russi, inoltre, continua Meduza, hanno perso l’accesso a una serie di servizi di uso quotidiano, come chiamare un taxi, effettuare pagamenti, ordinare consegne, controllare la posta elettronica. Fino al 13 ottobre, la stessa Yandex aveva comunicato ai propri utenti di star continuando a lavorare per ripristinare il funzionamento completo delle proprie attività.

Il Financial Times riporta che i disagi si sono estesi anche ai paesi confinanti con la Russia, con interruzioni dei servizi di posta elettronica, Yandex Pay e siti web che utilizzano l’infrastruttura dell’azienda russa in Kazakistan, Uzbekistan e Bielorussia. Nel 2024 Yandex era stata venduta forzatamente a investitori legati al presidente russo Vladimir Putin. All’epoca il vicepresidente della commissione parlamentare russa sull’informazione, Anton Gorelkin, aveva detto che «Yandex è più di un’azienda, è una risorsa per l’intera società russa».

articles.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
articles.summary: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
articles.preview: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday. Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at…
articles.body:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

articles.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
articles.summary: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
articles.preview: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt. Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.
articles.body:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well.

articles.body:
Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?

OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.

In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak, suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.

Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup, raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.”

Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August. Amazon has since filed an amended complaint.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems

This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon, which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok, Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are.

“Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge. “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.”

Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.

The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.”

The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.

While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.”

articles.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept
articles.summary: Mark Wahlberg, who once sank money into a gym chain that got kicked off the NYSE, is now building his own, and he promises you’ll get a cold plunge, a blood panel and a protein muffin without needing a trust fund.
articles.preview: Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness. Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December.
articles.body:
Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness.

Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing.

It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line.

The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt.

It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.”

By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.”

Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges. But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.”

Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership.

Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.”

When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand, for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.”

He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out).

Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “Wahl Street,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

“I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding, “I can’t understand that philosophy.”

The name Municipal is very intentional and clearly means a lot to Wahlberg, who grew up poor in Boston, one of nine kids, playing on public basketball courts and golf courses. “You learn a lot on the blacktop,” he said. “You learn to win, to lose, to compete, and hopefully to get back up and do it again.”

He has never hidden his rough youth. (He was sentenced to two years for assaults as a teenager and served 45 days.)

In fact, earlier in the afternoon on Thursday, surrounded by friends and business associates in a seating area backstage at Disrupt — this is the man who inspired the show “Entourage,” after all — he said he was turned around by two people, including Father Jim Flavin, a Boston-area parish priest who has been in Wahlberg’s life since he was 13.

He wants the gyms to carry that same spirit. “It’s a place to work, but have fun and support each other and create community and really challenge people to be better versions of themselves,” he said. “I’ve come from next to nothing to being in an amazing position,” Wahlberg continued. “I try to constantly remind myself that I can inspire other people growing up in similar situations, especially inner-city kids and at-risk youth, that there is a way to overcome your circumstances if you’re willing to go out there and do the work.”

At 55, his goals have changed, naturally. While he was once focused on looking good, “I just want to feel good when I wake up in the morning,” he said. “I want to be able to conquer all the things that I have planned for the day.”

He also said his plate is exceedingly full right now, between the gym, a film role as Pete Rose, and his daughter’s equestrian career. He’s so eager for the gym to open, he said, that visiting the construction site feels like “literally watching paint dry.” Indeed, asked if he was open to taking on new ventures, he shrugged. “I’m not out there hunting, looking for the next thing for sure.” But he wouldn’t rule it out, he added quickly. “If something amazing were to come along, obviously I wouldn’t turn it down.”

Pictured above with Walhberg, friend and business partner Bruce K. Lee.

articles.title: AI Trade Reversal Pierces Asia’s Star Picks-and-Shovels Stocks

articles.title: AI Selloff Tests Investor Confidence
articles.summary: Ritholtz Wealth Management Chairman and Chief Investment Officer Barry Ritholtz tells Bloomberg This Weekend that AI remains a transformational technology, but investors face a difficult task determining which companies will ultimately emerge as winners and losers. Speaking with hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini, Ritholtz discusses CoreWeave’s selloff, concerns about AI financing and valuations, and the challenges facing Tesla as competition in electric vehicles intensifies.

articles.title: La "Cernobbio delle donne" e la geopolitica dell'incertezza
articles.summary: AGI - "La Cernobbio delle donne " chiude il sipario con una platea di 500 manager e rappresentanti delle istituzioni che hanno animato la due giorni dedicata al tema della geopolitica dell'incertezza. La 26esima edizione del seminario internazionale " Donna, Economia & Potere ", organizzato dalla Fondazione Marisa Bellisario , si è svolta anche quest'anno presso le Corsie Sistine del complesso Santo Spirito in Sassia a Roma . Il tema scelto per quest'edizione, " Geopolitica dell'incertezza ", ha fatto da filo conduttore a due giorni di lavori che hanno riunito esperti, imprenditrici, rappresentanti istituzionali, ambasciatori, manager e giornalisti, articolati in 12 tavoli tematici . Fin dal suo esordio, l'appuntamento è stato appunto definito la " Cernobbio delle donne ". Lella Golfo: "La parità non è una concessione" Ad aprire i lavori è stata la presidente della Fondazione, Lella Golfo, che ha incentrato il suo intervento sul nesso tra leadership femminile e competitività del Paese. "La parità non è una concessione né un costo: è crescita, produttività, innovazione e una condizione indispensabile di competitività", ha dichiarato Golfo. "Il potere più autentico non è occupare uno spazio, ma allargarlo e rimandare giù l'ascensore per generare opportunità per le giovani". Sul fronte geopolitico, Golfo ha chiesto un' Europa più coesa : "Il futuro passa dalla pace", ha sottolineato, "e sulla guerra in Ucraina è arrivato il momento che l'Europa smetta di andare in ordine sparso e trovi un negoziato unico". Ha citato il rapporto Draghi sulla competitività come "un appello tanto applaudito quanto inascoltato" e ha messo in guardia sui rischi legati all'intelligenza artificiale: "L'IA è una forma di sovranità che rischia di essere progettata da un'industria a predominanza maschile, moltiplicando pregiudizi e stereotipi. Serve spingere le donne nelle materie STEM e nei luoghi in cui si scrive il codice del futuro". Un passaggio amaro è stato dedicato alla fuga dei giovani: "Oltre 630 mila ragazzi hanno lasciato l'Italia dal 2011 a oggi. Non è una semplice fuga, è un giudizio sulla mancanza di meritocrazia". Il messaggio di Papa Leone I lavori si sono aperti con la lettura, da parte di Golfo stessa, del messaggio inviato da Papa Leone XIV . "È per tutti noi un grande privilegio aprire i lavori di questa 26ª edizione con le parole del Santo Padre, che assicura il ricordo nella preghiera ed esorta alla testimonianza evangelica nei diversi settori professionali", ha detto Golfo. Nel testo, il Pontefice ha invocato la protezione della Vergine Maria e impartito la benedizione apostolica a tutti i partecipanti. La platea ha accolto le parole con un lungo applauso, in segno di vicinanza al Papa, ricoverato al Gemelli dopo l'asporto di un nodulo polmonare. Golfo ha rivolto a sua volta un pensiero al Pontefice: "Oggi il nostro pensiero e le nostre preghiere vanno al Santo Padre, a cui auguriamo di cuore buona salute". Il saluto di Giorgia Meloni Tra i messaggi istituzionali letti in apertura, ampio spazio ha avuto quello della Presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni. "Cara Lella, carissimi, anche quest'anno avete scelto di focalizzare l'attenzione sulle principali sfide della nostra epoca e di riflettere sulla profonda incertezza che caratterizza i nostri giorni", ha scritto Meloni. "La nostra Nazione può contare su una marcia in più . La risposta all'incertezza non è quella di chiudersi, ma di intessere nuove relazioni e saper guardare oltre gli schemi tradizionali". La premier ha ricordato il ruolo storico della Fondazione : "Ha reso visibili modelli che prima non lo erano e ha portato nel dibattito politico temi per troppo tempo rimasti marginali". Meloni ha poi fatto riferimento alla propria esperienza personale: "Il 25 ottobre di quattro anni fa, quando in Parlamento ho illustrato le dichiarazioni programmatiche del mio governo, ho ringraziato tutte quelle donne che con il loro esempio hanno costruito la scala che mi ha permesso di diventare la prima donna a ricoprire l'incarico di Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri. Marisa Bellisario appartiene a questa storia e da oltre 35 anni la Fondazione a lei intitolata continua ad aggiungere gradini perché le donne di oggi e di domani possano trovare la strada già aperta". I lavori aperti da Pichetto Fratin Il ministro dell'Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, ha aperto i lavori insieme a Golfo intervenendo su più fronti. Sul tema della parità di genere, ha preso le distanze dalle quote: "Non credo tanto alle quote quanto alla capacità del mondo donna. Non è uno spazio da dare, ma rendersi conto che la valutazione è di merito e quindi sono le donne che stanno conquistando quello che meritano", ha dichiarato. Sul dossier energetico e industriale, il ministro ha puntato il dito contro le politiche europee: "Credo sia abbastanza evidente, a livello europeo, un eccesso di ambizione che ha menomato il sistema dell'automotive. I percorsi di cambiamento verso la decarbonizzazione devono essere compatibili con la realtà e non eccessivamente ambiziosi, altrimenti il rischio è una crescita dell'inflazione per famiglie e imprese". La rotta indicata dal Governo per garantire competitività e sicurezza energetica punta sul "nuovo nucleare, per arrivare a quell'indipendenza e sicurezza energetica" necessarie a "dare speranza di futuro alle nuove generazioni". L'esortazione di Roberta Metsola Dal Parlamento Europeo sono arrivati due contributi distinti. La presidente Roberta Metsola, in un messaggio scritto, ha esortato le giovani donne: "Fatevi avanti, partecipate, candidatevi. Il cambiamento arriverà soltanto se sarete voi a renderlo possibile, altrimenti saranno gli altri a decidere per voi". Metsola ha ricordato i traguardi normativi ottenuti dall'Eurocamera (le direttive sull'equilibrio di genere nei consigli di amministrazione e sulla trasparenza retributiva) e ha lanciato un invito: "Portate le vostre proposte non solo a Roma, ma anche a Bruxelles e Strasburgo". Le parole di Antonella Sberna La vicepresidente del Parlamento Europeo Antonella Sberna, intervenuta alla tavola rotonda moderata dalla direttrice dell'AGI Rita Lofano , interrogata sulle prospettive dell'UE ha insistito sulla necessità di una politica estera comune: "L'Unione Europea in questo momento ha un' occasione storica che non ha mai avuto finora. Dobbiamo arrivare a una sola voce nella politica estera e di sicurezza comune", ha detto. "Nessuno di noi può fare a meno dell'Europa o augurarsi un'Europa debole". L'intervento di Daniela Fumarola La segretaria generale della Cisl, Daniela Fumarola, ha portato la prospettiva sindacale: "Non valorizzare il capitale umano femminile è un errore che impoverisce il Paese: se le donne fossero valorizzate, come è giusto che sia, il Pil aumenterebbe almeno del 6%", ha dichiarato. Sul tema della conciliazione, Fumarola ha sottolineato che "quando si ha un bambino, spesso la donna rinuncia al posto di lavoro per problemi di conciliazione . Bisogna invece condividere la genitorialità". Sulla manovra economica, la leader sindacale ha chiesto "un'ulteriore riduzione delle tasse sia sul lavoro sia sulle pensioni", indicando come priorità "lavoro, pensioni, famiglie e imprese sane che investono nonostante le crisi".

articles.preview: L’azienda di vendita di luce e gas entra nella produzione: obiettivo 25-30 MW in 2-3 anni. Focus su parchi fotovoltaici «Abbiamo un piano progressivo di investimenti in impianti su un orizzonte temporale di 2-3 anni con l’obiettivo di raggiungere una capacità di 25-30MW di energia rinnovabile, tendenzialmente fotovoltaica, per un impegno previsto fino a 30 milioni di euro nel periodo».
articles.body:
L’azienda di vendita di luce e gas entra nella produzione: obiettivo 25-30 MW in 2-3 anni. Focus su parchi fotovoltaici

«Abbiamo un piano progressivo di investimenti in impianti su un orizzonte temporale di 2-3 anni con l’obiettivo di raggiungere una capacità di 25-30MW di energia rinnovabile, tendenzialmente fotovoltaica, per un impegno previsto fino a 30 milioni di euro nel periodo».

Così Enrico Pozzi, presidente e ad di Compagnia Energetica Italiana (Cei), società milanese attiva da oltre dieci anni nella vendita di energia elettrica e gas, annuncia la scelta di integrare nel suo perimetro anche la produzione di elettricità.

Un passo che viene compiuto nel solco di una strategia industriale improntata all’equilibrio, alla prudenza, alla solidità. «Non facciamo trading. Non facciamo speculazione. Vendiamo gas ed elettricità alle stesse condizioni a cui compriamo. Abbiamo un portafoglio bilanciato che ci permette di garantire i nostri clienti. E ora facciamo un passo in più – racconta Pozzi –. Al posto di puntare sulla crescita dei clienti, che pure potremmo moltiplicare in poco tempo, riteniamo più interessante lavorare sul lato dell’approvvigionamento. Abbiamo cominciato acquisendo energia direttamente da produttori e ora aggiungiamo un ulteriore pezzo: nel nostro piccolo, vogliamo integrare produzione e vendita».

La mossa rappresenta un rafforzamento in un mercato che, dopo aver fatto i conti con i prezzi impazziti del 2022 all’inizio della guerra russa in Ucraina, si trova oggi a dover fronteggiare i rincari causati dalla crisi mediorientale e dello stretto di Hormuz: «Negli ultimi tempi il mercato è folle, se nel 2022 i valori sono saliti ma rimaneva coerenza tra prezzo, spread e circolante, quest’anno no. Ha senso per noi lavorare per aggiungere alla nostra azienda un pezzo che porti maggiore stabilità», indica Pozzi.

L’obiettivo della società sono impianti tendenzialmente fotovoltaici integrati con sistemi di accumulo a batteria, da acquistare e poi gestire. Con focus esclusivo sull’Italia e la prima operazione attesa entro la fine dell’anno, per poi cominciare l’attività concretamente a gennaio.

articles.title: Che cosa prevedono le regole europee sulla flessibilità richiesta dall’Italia
articles.summary: Il governo Meloni vuole margini di spesa più ampi per far fronte all’inflazione, ma si tratta di una richiesta distinta dalla clausola per difesa ed energia
articles.preview: Lunedì 12 ottobre, intervenendo all’assemblea di Assolombarda, la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni è tornata a parlare di flessibilità. «Quando abbiamo approvato i piani nazionali di bilancio, l’Europa lo ha fatto basandosi su un’inflazione programmata dell’1,8 per cento, ma oggi l’inflazione è molto più alta», ha detto Meloni, sostenendo che in vista del Consiglio europeo del 15 e 16 ottobre porterà «personalmente» la questione sul tavolo.

Lunedì 12 ottobre, intervenendo all’assemblea di Assolombarda, la presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni è tornata a parlare di flessibilità. «Quando abbiamo approvato i piani nazionali di bilancio, l’Europa lo ha fatto basandosi su un’inflazione programmata dell’1,8 per cento, ma oggi l’inflazione è molto più alta», ha detto Meloni, sostenendo che in vista del Consiglio europeo del 15 e 16 ottobre porterà «personalmente» la questione sul tavolo.

In sostanza, il governo italiano sostiene che l’aumento dei prezzi stia facendo crescere alcune spese dello Stato più di quanto previsto e chiede che l’Unione europea ne tenga conto quando valuta il rispetto delle regole europee sui bilanci pubblici. Ma che cosa chiede esattamente l’Italia? E che cosa prevedono le regole europee sulla flessibilità?

Per capirlo bisogna distinguere due richieste del governo Meloni: una riguarda le spese per difesa ed energia, che ha già ricevuto una valutazione favorevole dalla Commissione UE; mentre l’altra, attualmente in discussione, riguarda gli effetti dell’inflazione sui conti pubblici.
